children: The court found SBI had not properly considered the officer’s medical records or given him a fair opportunity before treating his absence as resignation

Patna High Court has ordered the reinstatement of a State Bank of India (SBI) officer who was treated as having voluntarily resigned after remaining absent from work because of illness. The court found that the bank had not properly considered his medical records or given him a fair opportunity to explain the absence before ending his service.
Pankaj Kumar Singh joined SBI in November 1989 and had completed more than 30 years of service. He was serving as deputy manager when he was transferred to the Muzaffarpur Zone in June 2019.

Singh was later diagnosed with acute jaundice and advised extended rest. He applied for leave and maintained that it had been sanctioned through the bank’s human resources management system for July 2019. His condition later worsened, requiring further treatment and bed rest until December.
After being declared fit, Singh reported for duty on 16 December 2019 but was informed that his leave had been declined.
SBI treated Singh’s absence from 29 June 2019 as unauthorised. In December 2019, the bank informed him that he had voluntarily left service, with the decision taking effect from 7 December.
His appeal was rejected in June 2020, after which he approached the Patna High Court seeking reinstatement.

The bank argued that Singh had remained absent for more than 90 consecutive days despite communications from management. Singh relied on his medical records and long service history to challenge the decision.
The High Court found no basis to treat Singh’s medical documents as false or fabricated. It also noted his claim that he had more than 270 days of earned leave.

The court held that these circumstances should have been considered before the bank treated the absence as voluntary resignation. It also found that Singh had not been given a fair opportunity to explain his absence.
The court quashed the bank’s notices and appellate order and directed SBI to reinstate Singh.
However, he will not receive salary or allowances for the period during which he did not work. That period will still count towards continuity of service.
The ruling highlights the need for employers to assess medical evidence and follow a fair process before treating prolonged absence as abandonment of employment.
